Open a workspace, edit code, run commands, and review changes from ChatGPT.

DevSpace brings a Codex-style coding loop to ChatGPT and other MCP hosts:
inspect the repo, follow local instructions, make scoped edits, run
verification, and show the user what changed.

## Open one workspace

Ask ChatGPT to open a project folder. Under the hood it calls `open_workspace`:

```json
{
  "path": "~/work/my-project"
}
```

The result includes a `workspaceId`. All later file, search, edit, show-changes,
and shell calls should reuse that same `workspaceId`.

Do not open the same checkout folder again unless:

- the `workspaceId` is rejected as unknown
- work moves to a different project folder
- work switches between checkout and worktree mode
- you ask for a new isolated worktree

## Checkout mode

Checkout mode is the default. DevSpace opens the actual directory.

Use this when you want ChatGPT to work in the current checkout.

## Worktree mode

Use worktree mode for isolated parallel work:

```json
{
  "path": "~/work/my-project",
  "mode": "worktree"
}
```

Managed worktrees live under `~/.devspace/worktrees`. Worktree mode requires a
Git repository with at least one commit. It starts from `HEAD` unless `baseRef`
is provided.

Each worktree-mode call creates a new managed worktree and returns a new
`workspaceId`. Uncommitted source checkout changes are not copied into the
managed worktree.

## Project instructions

When a workspace opens, DevSpace loads root-level instruction files:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `CLAUDE.md`

Nested instruction files are returned as available files. The model should read
the relevant nested file before working under that directory.

This keeps instructions explicit and inspectable instead of silently injecting
new context during later tool calls.

## Skills

Skills are enabled by default for coding-agent workflows.

DevSpace discovers standard Agent Skills from:

- `~/.agents/skills`
- project `.agents/skills`
- `~/.devspace/skills`

It also keeps compatibility with the bundled `subagents` skill when Subagents
are enabled.

## Typical loop

1. Open a workspace.
2. Inspect the tree and relevant files.
3. Follow project instructions and skills.
4. Make scoped edits.
5. Run tests or other verification.
6. Show changes for review.

You stay in the chat. DevSpace handles the local mechanics.

## Notes on policy

Using DevSpace as an MCP connector is a standard custom App/connector setup.
Your account is governed by your usage, not by DevSpace. Do not point it at
anything that would violate your provider's terms.

Where DevSpace is now and where it is going.

DevSpace is being built in public as an asymmetric bet on how agentic work will
actually run.

## The bet

Knowledge work will move into remote sandboxes. Models will get better at
meta-prompting and managing subagents under a budget. People will keep a matrix
of model preferences: big models for planning and review, smaller ones for
execution, mid ones for research.

DevSpace is the execution and orchestration layer for that world. Today it runs
on your machine. Later it can run in the cloud without changing the product
shape the host already knows.

## Now · v1.1

Local orchestrator.

- MCP server for ChatGPT and Claude
- workspace tools, Git worktrees, process sessions
- review widgets and change checkpoints
- bounded local subagent delegation
- explicit roots, Owner password, user-owned tunnels

This is the launch you are looking at.

## Next · v1.2

Dynamic workflow tooling.

The host should be able to write a loop programmatically and run a workflow
script. That script can sequence or parallelize fleets of local agents. You
discuss the work at a high level in ChatGPT or Claude. DevSpace runs the
delegation.

This is the step from "tools the host calls" to "orchestrator the host
directs."

## Later · v2

DevSpace Cloud.

Same tools. Same review. Same host. Remote sandboxes instead of only local
execution. That is the path to a paid product without abandoning the local-first
philosophy that makes v1 trustworthy.

## What stays true

- The host is the orchestrator.
- Everything happens in a workspace.
- Local authority stays explicit.
- Subagents are bounded workers.
- Prefer composable primitives over opaque autonomy.

If those stop being true, the product has drifted.

Install DevSpace and connect ChatGPT or Coding Agents.

This guide covers ChatGPT and Coding Agents using DevSpace with local projects.

## Requirements

- Node `>=22.19 <27`
- npm
- Git
- Bash, including Git Bash or WSL on Windows
- a public HTTPS URL that forwards to the local DevSpace server, only when
  ChatGPT will connect

DevSpace does not create the public tunnel for you. ChatGPT users can use
Cloudflare Tunnel, ngrok, Pinggy, Tailscale Funnel, or their own HTTPS reverse
proxy.

## Install and configure

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace init
```

Or install the CLI globally first:

```bash
npm install -g @waishnav/devspace
devspace init
```

The setup flow asks one question at a time.

First choose where you will use DevSpace: ChatGPT, Coding Agents, or both.
DevSpace uses that answer to skip setup that does not apply to you.

### Project roots

If you selected ChatGPT, choose the project folders it may open through
DevSpace. Keep this narrow.

Examples:

```text
~/personal,~/work
```

```text
/Users/alice/dev,/Users/alice/work
```

```text
C:\Users\alice\dev,C:\Users\alice\work
```

A Coding Agents-only setup skips this question. Direct `devspace agents`
commands use the current Git project, or the current directory outside a
repository, with the authority of your local shell. MCP workspace operations
remain limited to the roots configured for ChatGPT.

### Coding Agents

Setup detects supported Coding Agents and asks which ones DevSpace may use.
These choices are stored as provider objects under `subagents` in
`~/.devspace/config.json`.

If you selected Coding Agents, setup prints:

```bash
npx skills add Waishnav/devspace --skill subagents --global
```

The Skills CLI asks which installed Coding Agents should receive the skill.
The skill uses `devspace agents targets`, `run`, `continue`, `show`, and `ls`.
These commands do not require `devspace serve`.

### Connect ChatGPT

Setup only asks for a public URL if you selected ChatGPT. Start your tunnel or
reverse proxy first and point it at:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:7676
```

Enter the public origin without `/mcp`:

```text
https://your-tunnel-host.example.com
```

Configure the MCP client with the full MCP endpoint:

```text
https://your-tunnel-host.example.com/mcp
```

A Coding Agents-only setup skips this section.

## Start the server

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace serve
```

If your tunnel URL changes for one run, override it without rewriting config:

```bash
DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL="https://new-tunnel.example.com" npx @waishnav/devspace serve
```

For a stable public URL, persist it:

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace config set publicBaseUrl https://devspace.example.com
npx @waishnav/devspace serve
```

## Approve the client

When ChatGPT, Claude, or another MCP client connects, DevSpace shows an Owner
password approval page. Enter the Owner password printed during setup.

The default config files are:

```text
~/.devspace/config.json
~/.devspace/auth.json
```

Keep `auth.json` private.

## Check your setup

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace doctor
```

The doctor command reports the resolved config, Node version, Node ABI, platform,
Git, Bash, public URL, allowed hosts, and SQLite native dependency status.

## Platform support

| Platform | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | Supported | Requires Node, npm, Git, and Bash. |
| macOS | Supported | Requires Node, npm, Git, and Bash. |
| Windows with Git Bash, WSL, MSYS2, or Cygwin Bash | Supported | Git Bash is the simplest native Windows setup. |
| Windows PowerShell or `cmd.exe` only | Not supported yet | Install Git Bash or use WSL. |

## Running from a local checkout

If you are developing DevSpace itself instead of using the published package:

```bash
npm install --include=dev
npm run dev
```

The same setup rules apply.

Delegate bounded work to local coding agents through DevSpace.

Subagents are bounded workers. Each one has an explicit task, profile, working
context, lifecycle, and result that the host can inspect.

DevSpace coordinates them. The host decides when to delegate.

## Why subagents

Not every step belongs in the chat host's context window. Some work is better
done by a local coding agent with its own tools and session: implementing a
narrow change, running a focused investigation, or continuing an earlier agent
run.

DevSpace exposes that as inspectable delegation instead of a hidden loop.

## Profiles and targets

Setup detects supported Coding Agents and stores provider choices under
`subagents` in `~/.devspace/config.json`.

An agent profile is the model, provider, tools, and instructions used for a
subagent. Targets are the concrete agents DevSpace may launch on your machine.

## Skills CLI

For Coding Agents usage, setup prints:

```bash
npx skills add Waishnav/devspace --skill subagents --global
```

The skill uses:

- `devspace agents targets`
- `devspace agents run`
- `devspace agents continue`
- `devspace agents show`
- `devspace agents ls`

These commands do not require `devspace serve`.

## Boundaries

A subagent runs with local authority. Give it a clear task. Prefer small scopes.
Review the result before merging its work into something larger.

In v1.2, dynamic workflows will let the host write scripts that sequence or
parallelize fleets of these workers. Subagents are the unit that makes that
possible.

DevSpace is a local MCP execution layer for ChatGPT and Claude.

DevSpace is a self-hosted MCP server. It gives ChatGPT, Claude, and other MCP
hosts workspace-scoped tools for reading, editing, searching, running commands,
managing Git worktrees, reviewing changes, and coordinating bounded subagents on
your machine.

The host stays the orchestrator. DevSpace owns the mechanics.

## Why it exists

Chat interfaces are getting good at planning and deciding. They are still awkward
at touching a real project without uploading your tree somewhere else.

DevSpace keeps the work local. You approve which folders may open. You own the
tunnel. You approve each client with an Owner password. Inside an opened
workspace, the host can inspect the repo, make scoped edits, run shell commands,
and show you what changed.

## Mental model

1. Start your tunnel if ChatGPT will connect.
2. Run `devspace serve`.
3. Connect the MCP client to your public `/mcp` URL.
4. Approve the connection with the Owner password.
5. Ask the host to open a project inside one of your allowed roots.

From there, every file, search, edit, and shell call reuses the `workspaceId`
returned by `open_workspace`.

## What DevSpace is not

- It is not a hosted coding agent. The server runs on your machine.
- It is not a sandbox for shell. File tools are root-contained. Shell runs as you.
- It is not an opaque agent loop. Tools, workspaces, and subagents stay
  inspectable to the host.

## Product direction

**v1.1** is the local orchestrator you can run today.

**v1.2** adds dynamic workflows so the model can write and run scripts that
sequence or parallelize fleets of local agents.

**v2** is DevSpace Cloud: the same product shape with remote sandboxes when
local is not enough.

See the [roadmap](/guides/roadmap/) for more.

How DevSpace workspaces, roots, checkout mode, and worktrees fit together.

Everything in DevSpace happens in a workspace.

A workspace is one opened directory or worktree plus the instructions and state
accumulated while operating in it. It is not the same thing as an allowed root.

## Allowed roots

An allowed root is a configured filesystem boundary. ChatGPT may only open
workspaces inside those roots.

Keep roots narrow. Prefer `~/work` over `~`. Prefer a project folder over an
entire drive.

## Checkout vs worktree

**Checkout mode** opens the directory you already have. Edits land in that
checkout.

**Worktree mode** creates an isolated Git worktree under `~/.devspace/worktrees`.
Use it for parallel sessions or when you do not want the active checkout
touched.

Worktrees are a workflow boundary, not a security boundary.

## Workspace ID

`open_workspace` returns a `workspaceId`. Reuse it for every later call in that
session. Treat it as the handle for that opened context.

## Instructions and skills

Opening a workspace loads root instruction files and discovers skills. Nested
instruction files stay available for the model to read when work moves into a
subdirectory.

## Process sessions

Long-running commands become process sessions. The host can send input, read
output, or terminate them later. This keeps builds, servers, and interactive
tools inspectable instead of fire-and-forget.

How DevSpace surfaces outputs and native file downloads.

An artifact is an output surfaced for the host or user to inspect.

DevSpace keeps artifact handling explicit. It does not invent a hidden file
exchange service. When the host needs to pull a native file into a workspace, it
uses a documented one-shot download into an already-open workspace.

## Native file download

`download_artifact` accepts:

- the MCP host's native file value
- the `workspaceId` returned by `open_workspace`
- an unused relative destination path

It returns only the workspace-relative path. It does not create a persistent
artifact service or reusable artifact ID.

DevSpace accepts only the documented native-file object and trusted download
hosts and redirects. Arbitrary URL strings, local source paths, credentials,
malformed references, and unknown object fields are rejected.

## Failure modes

These fail closed:

- absolute paths
- path traversal
- symlinked parents
- existing destinations
- oversized transfers

Downloads stream under the configured per-file limit and are published without
overwrite as owner-only files. DevSpace does not extract or execute transferred
content.

## Review checkpoints

A review checkpoint is stored state representing a coherent set of changes. Use
it when you want the host or user to inspect a batch of edits as one unit
instead of reading every tool call in isolation.

## Logging

Artifact tool logs contain bounded workspace ID, validated hostname,
workspace-relative output path, byte count, hash, duration, and status metadata.
They do not log opaque file values, credentials, presigned URLs, host paths, or
file contents.

Config files, environment variables, and common DevSpace settings.

DevSpace stores local state under `~/.devspace/` by default.

```text
~/.devspace/config.json
~/.devspace/auth.json
~/.devspace/worktrees/
~/.devspace/skills/
```

Keep `auth.json` private. It holds the Owner password used to approve MCP
clients.

## Public base URL

ChatGPT needs a public HTTPS origin that forwards to the local server.

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace config set publicBaseUrl https://devspace.example.com
```

Or for one run:

```bash
DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL="https://new-tunnel.example.com" npx @waishnav/devspace serve
```

Use the origin only. Do not include `/mcp` in `publicBaseUrl`.

## Allowed roots

Roots are the filesystem boundaries ChatGPT may open. Prefer a short list of
project directories.

## Subagents

Provider choices from setup live under `subagents` in `config.json`. Re-run
`devspace init` or edit config when your local agent matrix changes.

## Useful commands

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace doctor
npx @waishnav/devspace config set publicBaseUrl https://example.com
npx @waishnav/devspace serve
```

## Environment overrides

Common overrides:

- `DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`
- `DEVSPACE_OAUTH_OWNER_TOKEN`
- `DEVSPACE_ALLOWED_HOSTS`
- `DEVSPACE_LOG_SHELL_COMMANDS`

Use `DEVSPACE_ALLOWED_HOSTS=*` only for intentional local debugging. Do not
enable shell command logging if commands may contain secrets.

For the full field-level reference, see the repository docs in
[`docs/configuration.md`](https://github.com/Waishnav/devspace/blob/main/docs/configuration.md).

Common setup and runtime traps when using DevSpace.

These are the problems people hit most often.

## Tunnel points at the wrong place

The tunnel should forward to `http://127.0.0.1:7676`, not the `/mcp` path.
Configure the MCP client with `https://your-host/mcp`. Put only the origin in
`publicBaseUrl`.

## Public URL includes `/mcp`

`DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` and `publicBaseUrl` are origins. If you paste the full
MCP URL there, OAuth metadata and host allowlisting get confused.

## Roots too broad

`~` or `/` make it hard to reason about access. Prefer specific project folders.

## Re-opening the same workspace

Reuse the `workspaceId`. Opening the same checkout again is usually wrong unless
the ID was lost, the project changed, or you intentionally want a new worktree.

## Assuming shell is sandboxed

File tools are root-contained. Shell is not. A connected host can run anything
your user can run.

## Worktrees are not a security boundary

They isolate workflow. They do not confine a hostile client.

## Coding Agents without serve

`devspace agents ...` commands work without `devspace serve`. ChatGPT still
needs the server and a public URL.

## Windows without Bash

PowerShell-only and `cmd.exe`-only setups are not supported yet. Install Git
Bash or use WSL.

## Changed tunnel URL

If the tunnel hostname changes, update `publicBaseUrl` or set
`DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` for that run. Then reconnect the MCP client.

## Doctor first

When something looks wrong, run:

```bash
npx @waishnav/devspace doctor
```

It reports the resolved config, Node, Git, Bash, public URL, allowed hosts, and
native dependency status.

How DevSpace treats roots, OAuth, tunnels, and shell access.

DevSpace exposes local coding capabilities over MCP. Treat it as remote access
to your development machine.

The security model is simple:

- you choose a narrow filesystem allowlist
- the MCP endpoint requires OAuth approval with your Owner password
- Host headers are allowlisted from the configured public URL
- every coding action happens through explicit MCP tool calls

## Filesystem allowlist

DevSpace only opens workspaces under configured roots.

Good examples:

```text
~/work
~/personal/open-source
```

Avoid broad roots:

```text
~
/
C:\
```

The narrower the root, the easier it is to reason about what the MCP client can
reach.

## Owner password

`devspace init` generates an Owner password and stores it in:

```text
~/.devspace/auth.json
```

When an MCP client connects, DevSpace shows an approval page. Enter the Owner
password only when you intentionally want that client to access this server.

For env-driven deployments, set a long random value:

```bash
DEVSPACE_OAUTH_OWNER_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
```

## Public URL and host allowlist

DevSpace needs `DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` so MCP clients can discover OAuth
metadata and connect to the correct resource.

The value should be the origin only:

```text
https://your-tunnel-host.example.com
```

Do not include `/mcp` in `DEVSPACE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`.

By default, DevSpace derives allowed Host headers from the local host and public
URL. Use `DEVSPACE_ALLOWED_HOSTS=*` only for intentional local debugging.

## Tunnels

DevSpace does not manage tunnels. Your tunnel or reverse proxy should point to:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:7676
```

Prefer adding Cloudflare Access, Tailscale identity controls, or equivalent
protection in front of public tunnels. DevSpace OAuth still protects the MCP
endpoint, but the tunnel URL should not be treated as a secret.

## Shell access

The shell tool is powerful by design. It is meant for tests, builds, git, and
package scripts.

Filesystem path containment applies to DevSpace file tools. Shell commands run
as local commands and can do what your user account can do. This is why the MCP
client must be trusted and the Owner password must stay private.

## Worktrees

Managed worktrees reduce accidental edits to your active checkout, but they are
not a security boundary. They are a workflow boundary for isolated coding
sessions.

## Native file download

Native file download is an opt-in, one-shot transfer into an already-open
workspace. Absolute paths, traversal, symlinked parents, and existing
destinations fail closed. Downloads stream under the configured per-file limit
and are published without overwrite as owner-only files. DevSpace does not
extract or execute transferred content.

## Logs

By default, DevSpace logs requests and tool calls. Shell command previews are
disabled unless `DEVSPACE_LOG_SHELL_COMMANDS=1`.

Do not enable shell command logging if commands may contain secrets.
